Subject: Finly discovery — p95 latency targets & streaming concurrency (recap + next steps)

Hi Samir / Jules —

Thanks again for taking the time today. Quick recap from our call so everyone has the same next steps and success criteria. Please flag anything I missed.

Key pain points you shared:
- Current RAG/assistant features are brittle at scale: user-facing response times spike during peak usage (esp. workflows with long context windows).
- Streaming UX is critical for customer-facing assistants — partial tokens must appear within ~150-250ms for a smooth experience.
- Backend concurrency: internal load tests show tail p95 latency degradation at ~150 concurrent streaming sessions.

Current stack (what you told us):
- Inference hosted on a self-managed Kubernetes cluster using off-the-shelf endpoints (single-model replicas).
- Model: mix of open Llama-3 variants and a few ensemble reranking calls.
- No persistent KV cache today; custom prefix caching is in early experiments.

Success criteria (agreed):
- p95 token response latency <= 200ms for short-turn streaming (first bytes within 150-250ms ideally).
- Sustained concurrency of 150 streaming sessions with acceptable p95 (<=200ms) during peak.
- End-to-end user-perceived latency improvement of 30% on key assistant flows.

Proposed next steps:
1) Share the call deck + sample latency logs (attached).
2) Technical deep-dive with Aditya and your infra team next week to validate real traffic patterns and concurrency shapes.
3) Pilot on Dedicated capacity (or our private VPC) with prefix caching + batching enabled to measure p95 improvements.
4) Demo streaming primitives (token-by-token) and show UX improvements live.

Attachments: Finly-discovery-deck-20261210.pdf, latency-sample-logs-20261210.csv

I'll coordinate with Aditya on availability for a deep-dive. Ideal window from your side?

Best,
Marissa

Thanks Marissa — this looks great and matches our notes. A few clarifications from our side: 

- Targeting p95 <= 200ms is correct for short responses (under ~200 tokens). For longer reads (400+ tokens) we expect slightly higher per-token times but still need stable tails.
- Our production traffic during the 8–10AM PST spike shows roughly 140–180 concurrent active streaming sessions hitting the assistant. Spiky tail events come from concurrent reranker calls (3x per session) and some heavier context sizes (1000+ tokens).
- We can share a week of traffic samples if it helps the pilot.

We're available for a technical deep-dive Tues or Wed next week (Dec 15/16) between 9:30–12:30 PST. Prefer Dec 16 if Aditya is available.

Hi Samir / Jules —

Thanks for the clarity on concurrency shape and reranker behavior. A few notes from a technical standpoint ahead of the deep-dive: 

- Root causes we've seen for p95 tail: small-batch execution on GPUs during peaks, KV cache cold starts, and multi-call reranker patterns. Redwood levers to address these: continuous batching, KV/prefix cache, and smart routing to model variants during spikes.
- For streaming UX, we can ensure first-byte delivery (via partial token flush) in the 120–220ms window depending on model and GPU type; optimizing kernel selection and shorter initial decode steps helps.
- Recommended pilot config for realistic measurement:
  * Dedicated capacity (reserved pool) sized to support 160 concurrent streamers with 30% buffer.
  * Enable prefix KV caching for hot contexts (reduces token compute for repeated prefixes).
  * Configure batching window to 10–25ms with concurrency-aware thresholds to avoid latency surprises.
  * Use a BARELY-QUANTIZED variant for reranker where accuracy matters, or route reranks to smaller replicas if throughput is the bottleneck.

Can you share redirects for your synthetic load test or a sampling job so we can mirror the traffic shape? Also, if you have a sample of reranker call frequency per session, that will help size the pilot correctly.

I can set aside Dec 16 at 10:00 AM PST for the deep-dive — planning to bring one of our runtime engineers to measure expected p95s given your traces.
